stem: A software vendor has 60 developers split into frontend, backend and data teams. People move between teams every few months, and each team needs a different, stable set of permissions. Which authorization design needs the least administrative effort?

choices.text: Attach inline policies to each developer's IAM user and edit those policies whenever someone changes teams
Create a parent IAM group that contains the three team groups so that shared permissions are inherited by each team
Name each team's IAM group as the Principal in the resource-based policies on that team's buckets and queues
Create one IAM group per team with a managed policy attached, and move users between groups when they change teams

rationale: IAM user groups let you attach a policy once and give it to every member; when someone changes jobs you remove them from the old group and add them to the new one instead of editing their permissions. Inline policies have a one-to-one relationship with a single identity, so 60 copies would need editing on every move. IAM groups can't be nested; a group contains only users, not other groups. A group cannot be a Principal in a resource-based policy, because groups relate to permissions, not authentication.
